newsitem.title: FRANCE: South Korean minister confident on OECD vote.
newsitem.headline: South Korean minister confident on OECD vote.

text.p: South Korean Foreign Minister Gong Ro-Myung said on Friday he was confident that a vote to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development would be secured in December despite stiff opposition party resistance.
"It is true there are some views in Korea, particularly in the opposition, that the time for accession is not particularly appropriate," Gong told a news conference at the OECD here.

But even if the economy was slowing this year after a sustained period of strong growth, "it is high time Korea was accepted", he said after a ceremony to mark the invitation of South Korea to become the second Asian member of the OECD.

"I am pretty confident we can have the accession concurred," Gong said when asked if the government, which has a narrow majority in the national assembly, was certain of overcoming parliamentary opposition to the move.
"We now have a final hurdle back home."

Gong ran through a hefty list of South Korea's achievements, saying it had been transformed from one of the world's poorest economies before an industrialisation drive in the 1960s and now had the 11th biggest output in the world.
"Entry into the OECD is not our final goal, but a starting point for further liberalisation of the economy," he said.

Gong said he expected the motion ratifying OECD membership to be submitted to the national assembly next week. "We expect by the end of the current session (on December 18) to obtain the national assembly's concurrence," he added.

Questioned on South Korea's progress on opening the economy, OECD secretary general Donald Johnson said: "One of the major benefits is peer group pressure, constantly pushing you to move further and further down the path of liberalisation. Korea has made the commitment."
Gong said Seoul would raise limits on foreign investment by outsiders in firms to 20 percent in 1996 and 23 percent in 1997.

Gong, who said he needed a simple majority to ensure OECD membership was ratified in parliament, faces resistance from opposition groups who warn that the OECD could force it to speed up the pace at which it opens local markets to offshore competition.

A major lobby group, the Citizens Coalition for Economic Justice, has promised a nationwide campaign against membership of the OECD, a research and debating forum which is spreading its message of free-market economics beyond the traditional reserve of the richer industrialised nations.
Gong used a separate address to OECD representatives to remind them of his country's division with North Korea.
"Six years ago the world watched with deep emotion as the Berlin Wall tumbled down and the two Germany's were reunified," he said in his cermonial speech.

"Continents away, however, the Korean people are still divided and the DMZ remains a formidable reminder of the frigid Cold War confontation. The recent infiltration by a North Korean submarine into our territory constitutes a serious threat to the peace and stability of the Korean peninsula," he said.

"It is my most sincere hope that Korea will be able to accomplish reunification in the near future. In this respect, we wish to count on the full understanding and support of the OECD member countries," he said, according to a text of the speech.
South Korea would expand OECD membership to 29 on the heels of Poland and give it a greater weight in Asia, where long-time member Japan has been the region's only member to date.
